rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ascension prefigures the transfer of the two holy houses from dishonest custodians to people who will fulfil their purpose.
rows.anchor: the custodianship of these houses of God will now be entrusted to those who will fulfil their real objective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening glorification and closing divine attributes rebuke people who imagine God is unaware; accountability is near and He judges with perfect knowledge.
rows.anchor: Time is now near for their accountability. It is God Who actually sees and hears

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for night journey inherently means travelling at night; with the preposition bi it means taking someone somewhere at night, while laylan emphasizes the time.
rows.anchor: is an inherent part of this word, yet at times this word occurs without this qualification

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Applying the night-journey verb to the Prophet expresses explicit distinction, God's affection for him, and his perfection as God's servant.
rows.anchor: evidences explicitness for him, God’s extreme love and affection for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Prophet God's servant is the most specific and sufficient description of his personality.
rows.anchor: pinpoints in a very specific manner the person who bests represents it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sacred Mosque is the Ka‘bah; the distant mosque is Jerusalem, about forty days from Makkah, in a land blessed materially for fertility and spiritually as home to many prophets.
rows.anchor: This distant mosque was situated in Jerusalem at a distance of about 40 days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The journey's stated purpose is to show the Prophet grand divine signs; it signals that the holy sites will be taken from dishonest custodians and entrusted to him.
rows.anchor: the glad tidings of help and support that were being given to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse first withholds the speaker to convey the event's majesty, then names the speaker to express affection and attention.
rows.anchor: The earlier part of the verse did not reveal the speaker which signifies the majesty of an event

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ascension further strengthened the Prophet's assurance of divine support during a difficult phase and showed him what would happen.
rows.anchor: were further strengthened by this journey of his ascension and he was also shown what was to transpire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the signs shown during the journey as a true prophetic dream, since 17:60 calls the vision a dream; exegetes likewise identify it with this event.
rows.anchor: that dream We showed you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic dreams are a means of divine revelation, alongside God's communication through angels.
rows.anchor: such true dreams are a means of God’s revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic dreams are unmistakably clear to the prophet, and God also explains any symbolic element.
rows.anchor: such dreams absolutely clear and unambiguous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dreams effectively let prophets observe detailed facts and incidents, including meanings that are difficult to convey in words.
rows.anchor: This is the most effective way when the purpose is to make a prophet observe certain facts and incidents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True dreams convey broader and more certain understanding than eyesight, which is limited and can deceive; Moses could not see God's manifestation with his eyes, while Muhammad could observe what was shown without being dazed.
rows.anchor: true dreams carry no deception. Eyes can only see in a limited scope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rebukes Jewish claims to exclusive religious leadership by descent from Jacob; they rejected prophets outside their race and opposed Muhammad, whose Ascension report intensified their anger.
rows.anchor: the arrogant notion of the Jews that they are the progeny of Jacob

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No nation earns God's favour through lineage; faith and righteous deeds are what merit His blessings.
rows.anchor: It is faith and righteous deeds which earn them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israelite scripture predicted two episodes of major rebellion and defeat; history fulfilled the warnings, with mercy after reform and punishment after renewed disorder.
rows.anchor: these predictions materialized word for word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same choice faces the Jews addressed in this sūrah: accepting God's messenger brings a share in his blessings, while rejection invites punishment.
rows.anchor: God’s messenger has opened the way to success and salvation for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God truly hears and sees; others have only the limited faculties He grants, so the claim warns Quraysh idolaters and Israelites that their deeds are known.
rows.anchor: only God actually hears and sees. Nothing is beyond his hearing and sight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is the Torah; wali means a guardian or helper to whom one entrusts all affairs in complete confidence.
rows.anchor: a guardian and helper and someone who can be consigned all of one’s affairs by completely trusting him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address introduces the Jews' wrong beliefs: they ignored God's elaborate scriptural guidance and fell into polytheism despite its explicit prohibition.
rows.anchor: They completely ignored His scripture of guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism is foundational to every religious teaching and the whole sharī‘ah; holding to it means holding to religion, while losing it loses religion.
rows.anchor: The entire sharī‘ah is based on it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah is replete with monotheism, so Islahi offers one biblical quotation rather than prolonging the discussion with many references.
rows.anchor: the whole Torah is replete with the teaching of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic ban on taking another guardian parallels the Bible's ban on worshipping other gods; despite this clear command, Jews repeatedly fell into polytheism and their prophets rebuked them.
rows.anchor: How similar are the Qur’ ānic words “Do not make anyone your guardian except Myself”

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Islahi cites Jesus as rebuking Israelites with the saying that they had omitted adultery on the first night; the translator says he could not find its reference.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) went as far as to say: “O Israelites! You have omitted adultery the first night.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative particle “O” is omitted; the Israelites are reminded that they descend from Noah's people, whom God saved in the Ark.
rows.anchor: The particle of invocation (O!) is suppressed here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Noah was grateful, his descendants should show gratitude by adhering to monotheism; Noah's polytheistic people were destroyed, and Israel faces the same consequence if it follows them.
rows.anchor: Noah (sws) was a grateful person, they too should show gratitude and adhere to monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition after “We decreed” implies a missing verb such as “We informed,” yielding the sense that God informed Israel after making His decision.
rows.anchor: The translation would thus be: We informed the Israelites after taking this decision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The Book” encompasses all scriptures given to Israelite prophets, not only the Torah; David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Jesus warned about the two disorders and their outcomes.
rows.anchor: this word has been used for the Torah as well as for the scriptures of other prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disorders mean rebellion against God's monotheism and sharī‘ah. Although Israel's history includes other disorder, this passage concerns two defeats that humiliated and routed the whole nation.
rows.anchor: Disorder means rebellion against monotheism and the sharī‘ah of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David's Psalm 106 describes the first disorder: Israel adopted foreign customs and idols, sacrificed children, and was handed over to hostile nations.
rows.anchor: He gave them into the hands of the nations, and their foes ruled over them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects Jesus' warning that Jerusalem's temple stones would be thrown down, and his lament over Jerusalem's coming suffering, to the second disorder.
rows.anchor: Following are the words of Jesus (sws) regarding the prophecy of the second disorder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words meaning “We will punish you twice” are omitted because their implication is clear and the following verses supply the details.
rows.anchor: the complete sense would be: We had informed the Israelites in the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle idha can express an established practice or portray a situation, not only refer to the future; Islahi takes it in the latter sense here.
rows.anchor: not merely used for the future; it is also used to express an established practice and convention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition after the verb adds the sense of letting someone loose upon another, alongside stirring up.
rows.anchor: besides “stirring up” this verb encompasses the meaning of “letting loose someone on someone.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An enemy able to enter homes has violated all respect and honour; the later wording will note the further violation of the Aqṣā Mosque.
rows.anchor: if the enemy is so powerful that it barges into houses, this means that it has totally violated all respect and honour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first punishment refers to Nebuchadnezzar’s attack, which devastated Jerusalem in 586 BC; Islahi cites Jeremiah’s warning and lament over the city’s ruin.
rows.anchor: This is a reference to the attack of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jeremiah's lament in Lamentations portrays God's anger bringing down Judah's strongholds, kingdom, princes, and Israel's power.
rows.anchor: He has brought her kingdom and its princes down to the ground in dishonour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar's army is called God's servants because it served as an instrument of His will, not because it was pious; God used these filthy people to remove a great pile of filth.
rows.anchor: These words are not used because of their piety and religiosity but because they served as tools and weapons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against Israel's claim to be God's favoured children, the invaders who beat them had standing with God while Israel had none.
rows.anchor: the shoes by which they have been beaten have some weight with God but they have none whatsoever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Israel reformed following years of helplessness, God restored its fortunes through Cyrus's defeat of the Chaldeans in 539 BC and permission for exiles to return.
rows.anchor: they were once again helped by Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel's emancipation after slavery should have taught it the lesson of the verse, but events unfolded as the prophecy had foretold.
rows.anchor: Even their prophets fully informed them of this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ellipsis before the second attack is signalled by the definite article, which points back to the mighty people mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: distinctly points to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biblical history identifies the second destruction of the Jews with Emperor Titus's attack in 70 CE, as Jesus had foretold.
rows.anchor: the destruction of the Jews at the hands of the Roman Emperor Titus in 70 AD

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word translated “shed” means a shelter or pen where animals are kept.
rows.anchor: The word E  refers to a shed in which animals are kept

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews in the Prophet's time backed Quraysh against the Qur’an and are urged to accept the unlettered Prophet: reform brings mercy, renewed evil brings punishment, and Hell awaits beyond worldly humiliation.
rows.anchor: they should adhere to the message of this unlettered prophet that has been sent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from indirect to direct: the first clause dismisses the Jews' choice as affecting only themselves, while the direct, elliptical warning is especially stern.
rows.anchor: The first part has a ring of disregard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section III invites Jews and Quraysh to the Qur’an's natural straight path, contrasts the fates of acceptance and rejection, rebukes those blind to signs who demand punishment, and alludes to God's practice of punishing nations.
rows.anchor: both the Jews and the Idolaters of the Quraysh are invited to profess faith in the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word qawim means straight: a path aligned with human nature and intellect that leads to God.
rows.anchor: It refers to the path which is in exact harmony with human nature and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an calls Jews and Quraysh to abandon wandering and follow its path; it promises a great reward to righteous believers and painful torment to deniers of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: If they want to reach God, they should leave aside wandering here and there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts Qur’an's rivals demanding a punishment sign instead of accepting it; their foolish, destructive demand is described indirectly to express sorrow.
rows.anchor: This is a depiction of the rivals of the Qur’ ān who instead of professing faith in it were demanding a sign of punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rather than using their respite to reform, the rivals make a naïve demand for punishment.
rows.anchor: instead of benefitting from the respite and reforming themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day are signs directed to those demanding punishment; their precise succession distinguishes time, enables year-counting and calculation, and night offers rest while day lets people seek God's bounty.
rows.anchor: from the succession of the night and day with such precision people are able to find the count of years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's provision of every necessary detail in the Qur’an is another favour, making the Book sufficient for those who deliberate.
rows.anchor: every necessary detail has been provided to them in this Book of theirs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the Qur’an draws monotheism from night and day's harmonious opposites and the Hereafter from their succession; Islahi discusses these proofs elsewhere in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: it has adduced monotheism from the harmony between day and night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṭā’ir literally means bird; because Arabs sought omens and the future from birds, it came to mean fate or future.
rows.anchor: since the Arabs used it as an omen and portent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Judgment no soul bears another's burden; each person sees and carries the burden of their own deeds.
rows.anchor: Every person will observe his deeds and carry their burden alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The last clause further explains that God does not punish a nation before sending a messenger to establish the truth conclusively.
rows.anchor: Before they are punished, He sends them a messenger to conclusively deliver the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first clause suppresses the idea that God made night dark for comfort, as the later clause about seeking His bounty implies.
rows.anchor: The meaning would be: We made the night dark so that you receive comfort from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those demanding punishment are rebuked for haste: a messenger has arrived, and only his conclusive delivery of the truth remains; failing to use this respite will bring ruin.
rows.anchor: A messenger has come to them to conclusively deliver the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amr can mean giving respite as well as commanding; the imperative here actually grants people time after the truth has been established, leaving no excuse.
rows.anchor: An imperative style is apparently adopted here, but it actually implies giving respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affluent are given this respite because they control society and are addressed first by messengers; their obstinacy and pursuit of the messenger's death lead to his migration and the nation's punishment.
rows.anchor: This respite is given to the affluent because they have the reins of the society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse further explains God's established practice regarding nations sent messengers.
rows.anchor: The verse is a further explanation of the established practice of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past nations corroborate this divine practice; the verse assures the Prophet that God knows his people's crimes and will not delay punishment when its time arrives.
rows.anchor: This is a further corroboration to the just referred to the established practice of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-‘ājilah contrasts with the Hereafter and means this world and its immediate gains.
rows.anchor: is used in contrast to the hereafter and hence refers to this world and to is immediate gains

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi flags God's choosing who receives immediate worldly benefits and in what quantity as central to His practice of giving respite; this extract cuts off before his explanation.
rows.anchor: need to be specially kept in mind
